title: Xylitol: What It Is, How It Differs From Sugar, and Where You Usually Find It

seo.title: Xylitol: Calories, Teeth, and How It Differs From Sugar
seo.meta_description: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol with sweetness similar to sugar but less usable energy. It produces a smaller glucose response and does not promote tooth decay like sucrose, so it is common in sugar-free gum. Large doses can cause GI symptoms, and xylitol is highly toxic to dogs.
seo.search_intent: Understand what xylitol is, how it compares with sugar in sweetness, calories, glucose response, and dental effects, where it is used, and what safety cautions matter.

excerpt: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol with sweetness close to sucrose. European labeling assigns polyols such as xylitol 2.4 kcal/g, versus about 4 kcal/g for sugar. It produces a smaller glucose response and oral bacteria do not use it the way they use sucrose, which is why it is common in sugar-free gum and oral-care products. High doses can cause GI symptoms, and xylitol is highly toxic to dogs.
content_html:
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol whose sweetness is close to that of sucrose but whose metabolism is different. It is especially common in sugar-free gum, mints, candy, tabletop sweeteners, and oral-care products.

Unlike stevia or saccharin, xylitol is not hundreds of times sweeter than sugar. It is used in gram quantities, contributes bulk, and creates a characteristic cooling sensation as it dissolves.

Xylitol provides less energy than sucrose

European nutrition labeling assigns 2.4 kcal/g to polyols other than erythritol. Sucrose provides about 4 kcal/g.

That is roughly a 40% reduction per gram in the European calculation. It can reduce a product's calories, but the finished food may still contain substantial fat, flour, nuts, or other energy sources.

Xylitol-sweetened does not mean calorie-free.

Its blood-glucose response is generally smaller

Xylitol is incompletely absorbed and does not produce the same rapid glucose rise as an equivalent amount of sucrose. This makes it useful when manufacturers want sweetness with a lower glycemic effect.

The entire food still matters. A xylitol cookie can contain starch, and a sugar-free chocolate can contain substantial fat and other carbohydrates.

An ingredient's glycemic behavior should not be treated as a complete diabetes recommendation for the finished product.

Why is xylitol so common in gum and dental products?

Cavity-associated oral bacteria do not ferment xylitol the same way they ferment sucrose and other cariogenic sugars. Sugar-free chewing gum also stimulates saliva, which helps neutralize acids and support enamel remineralization.

FDA notes broadly that sugar alcohols do not promote tooth decay like traditional sugars. This is one reason xylitol has become strongly associated with gum, mints, and oral-care products.

It does not replace fluoride toothpaste, brushing, flossing, or dental care.

Large amounts can cause GI symptoms

Unabsorbed xylitol reaches the colon, where some fermentation occurs. Polyols also exert an osmotic effect that can draw water into the bowel.

High intakes can therefore cause gas, bloating, rumbling, or diarrhea. Tolerance varies, and a large amount consumed quickly is more likely to cause problems.

European foods containing more than 10% added polyols must warn that excessive consumption may produce laxative effects.

Xylitol is highly dangerous to dogs

Dogs regulate xylitol very differently from humans. Even relatively small exposures can trigger a rapid insulin release and severe hypoglycemia; larger exposures can also cause serious liver injury.

Sugar-free gum, candy, peanut or nut spreads, baked products, and dental products containing xylitol should be stored where pets cannot reach them. Suspected dog ingestion is a veterinary emergency.

The canine toxicity mechanism should not be extrapolated to humans.

What about the recent cardiovascular study?

A 2024 study reported an association between higher circulating xylitol and cardiovascular events in high-risk cohorts and also found acute effects on platelet responsiveness in laboratory and small human experiments.

This is a research signal, not proof that ordinary dietary xylitol causes heart attacks or strokes. Circulating xylitol can also reflect endogenous metabolism and underlying health state, so blood concentration is not a simple measure of how much gum or sweetener someone consumed.

EFSA's re-evaluation of E 967 remains ongoing in 2026, so it is appropriate to describe the emerging evidence without inventing a final regulatory conclusion.

Where xylitol usually appears

Look for it in sugar-free chewing gum, mints, candy, throat lozenges, tabletop sweeteners, some nut spreads, and oral-care products. It can also be part of a mixed-polyol system in confectionery.

For people who use xylitol mainly for dental reasons, frequency and context matter too. A piece of sugar-free gum after a meal is a very different exposure from eating a large bag of polyol-sweetened candy in one sitting, both for oral benefit and gastrointestinal tolerance.

The practical rule: xylitol can replace sugar with lower energy and lower cariogenic potential, but it is not unlimited. Large amounts can cause digestive symptoms, and every xylitol-containing product should be kept away from dogs.

faq.question: How many calories does xylitol have?
faq.answer: European labeling uses 2.4 kcal/g for polyols such as xylitol, compared with about 4 kcal/g for sucrose.

faq.question: Is xylitol good for teeth?
faq.answer: It is not fermented by cavity-causing bacteria like sugar and is useful in sugar-free gum, but it does not replace fluoride and oral hygiene.

faq.question: Is xylitol toxic to dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. It can cause severe hypoglycemia and liver injury in dogs and requires urgent veterinary attention after ingestion.
